headline: High: LightAgent’s broad egress/MCP and secret-handling can amplify unsafe cross-agent data flow; prompt-injection and cascading-error risks are also present.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A has no documented shared channel, but Agent B exposes MCP/stdin-stdout and can run browsers/subprocesses, so if A’s outputs are bridged into B they may be treated as instructions. The pairwise pathway is inferred rather than directly documented, so uncertainty pushes above low.
conditions: IF Agent A outputs are copied into Agent B via MCP, stdin/stdout, or files
IF Agent B parses A-generated text as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable automatic handoff from A to B
Add a provenance tag to all A outputs before B reads them
Require B to treat A text as untrusted data
Review any MCP prompt templates for instruction-like delimiters

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent B touches user conversations, memory, trace data, tool calls, and secrets, while Agent A is open-source docs-only with no egress. If they share a workspace or if A forwards content into B, B’s broad egress can leak sensitive material. The shared-storage path is not documented, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF Agent A and Agent B share files, transcripts, or memory state
IF Agent B sends any shared content to external APIs or browsers
mitigations: Keep A and B in separate workspaces
Strip secrets from any handoff payloads
Disable B network egress for sensitive runs
Rotate any API keys exposed to B
Log and review all B outbound requests

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent B supports multiple instances and broad network/tool use; Agent A is docs-only and has no write surfaces listed, so direct write-write conflict is not proven. However, B’s concurrency plus shared MCP/tooling can still collide on shared mutable resources if the orchestrator exposes them, so uncertainty warrants medium.
conditions: IF both agents are granted the same mutable workspace or OAuth scope
IF the orchestrator does not provide locking around shared resources
mitigations: Assign separate resource scopes per agent
Enable locking on shared files or tokens
Run only one B instance per mutable target
Audit overlapping OAuth scopes
Use read-only mounts for A

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent B can consume tool results and workflow state, so if A’s outputs are forwarded into B without verification, B may act on incorrect or hallucinated content. A has no documented verification or action controls, and B’s tool-use stack makes downstream propagation plausible. This is an interaction risk in default-style pipelines, not a proven high-severity action chain.
conditions: IF B treats A’s output as authoritative input
IF no human or programmatic verification step exists before B acts
mitigations: Insert a verification step between A and B
Require citations or source links for A claims
Have B cross-check critical outputs against original sources
Block action-taking until a human approves
Record provenance metadata on every forwarded item

E_compliance.rationale: Agent B explicitly handles secrets, conversations, memory, and trace data, while Agent A is docs-only and open-source with no data classes listed. If regulated data is routed into B, retention/residency and secret-handling obligations can diverge; A is not the compliance driver here, so only B is cited for the concrete exposure surface.
conditions: IF regulated personal data or secrets are routed into Agent B
IF retention or residency rules differ from the operator’s policy
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from B runs
Set short retention on B logs and traces
Mask secrets before tool calls
Document data residency for B’s backend
Use a separate compliant environment for sensitive workflows
